The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, a readily accessible surrogate biomarker for insulin resistance and metabolic health, has been extensively investigated across various ethnic populations. The critical role of physical activity (PA) in enhancing insulin sensitivity has been corroborated by numerous studies. Nonetheless, the relationship between different patterns of PA and the TyG index remains ambiguous. This study seeks to elucidate the association between different PA patterns and the TyG index. Participants with complete data on TyG index, PA patterns, and other covariates from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey database (2007–2018) were included in this study. Participant characteristics across PA groups were compared using Rao-Scott chi-squared test or Kruskal–Wallis test. Multivariate linear regression models were used to assess the relationship between PA patterns and the TyG index, with subgroup analyses, interaction tests and restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression analyses conducted to explore the stability and potential nonlinearity of PA-TyG index association, respectively. A total of 16,440 participants were included, with 12,909, 164, 118, and 3249 individuals being inactive, insufficiently active, weekend warriors (WWs), and regularly active (RA), respectively. Multivariate adjusted linear regression models showed that insufficiently active adults (β = − 0.05, P = 0.3524), WWs (β = −0.01, P = 0.9129), and RA adults (β = − 0.110, P < 0.0001) all had significantly lower TyG indices compared to inactive adults. Significant difference was observed between WWs and RA adults ( P for trend < 0.0001). Stratified analyses and interact tests revealed that the PA-TyG index association in RA group was more pronounced in individuals being male, with higher education levels, and without diabetes. Additionally, a significant, non-linear, and negative relationship between weekly total PA and TyG index in non-inactive individuals was determined by RCS analysis ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.054). Being regularly active is linked to a substantial reduction in the TyG index, whereas weekend warriors and those with insufficient activity do not experience comparable benefits. Nevertheless, the weekend warrior approach can provide a practical alternative for individuals who are unable to engage in consistent exercise. Keywords Weekend warrior Triglyceride-glucose index Physical activity NHANES Cross-sectional study Subject terms Diabetes Public health Natural Science Foundation of Guangdong Province K20113077 K20113077 K20113077 Zhang JinYe Zheng HaoNan Yu Bin issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Limited 2025 Introduction Physical activity (PA) is imperative for individuals of all ages to promote proper growth and development, enhance physical and cognitive function, improve sleep quality, and decrease the likelihood of chronic diseases 1 . According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 18–64 year-old adults are strongly suggested to perform 150–300 min of moderate-intensity aerobic PA, or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic PA, or an equivalent combination of both throughout the week for the harvest of substantial health benefits 2 . In recent years, since leisure time physical activity on weekends may be a more convenient option for many people, an increasing number of individuals have chosen to focus on 1 or 2 physical activities per week, known as “Weekend Warriors” (WWs) 3 . A large prospective cohort study suggested that individuals who engage in active physical activity patterns, whether weekend warriors or regular exercisers have lower all-cause and cause-specific mortality rates than inactive individuals do 4 . However, it is unclear whether concentrating on physical activity over one or two days (known as the weekend warrior pattern) can achieve the same benefits as exercising regularly. Insulin resistance (IR) has been proved to correlate with increased risks of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, etc., while PA has been demonstrated to be one of the most reliable strategies to alleviate IR 5 . iors or regular exercisers have lower all-cause and cause-specific mortality rates than inactive individuals do 4 . However, it is unclear whether concentrating on physical activity over one or two days (known as the weekend warrior pattern) can achieve the same benefits as exercising regularly. Insulin resistance (IR) has been proved to correlate with increased risks of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, etc., while PA has been demonstrated to be one of the most reliable strategies to alleviate IR 5 . The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a simple, convenient, and low-cost marker of IR that does not require insulin quantification 6 – 8 . This index can be calculated simply by fasting triglycerides and fasting glucose in routine biochemical tests and is not restricted by insulin therapy 9 . In recent years, several studies have shown that the TyG index can be used to identify individuals at risk for developing diabetes in the future and presents is associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD), stroke, depression, and sleep disorders 10 – 14 . However, whether the TyG index, an index closely related to health, can be improved by physical activity (PA) is unknown. Also, it is unclear whether there is a correlation between PA patterns and the TyG index, and whether the benefits of different PA patterns are similar. Therefore, we investigated the relationship between PA patterns and the TyG index via a cross-sectional study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohort. This study aimed to increase of the positive impact of exercise patterns on the TyG index and to provide recommendations for adopting different activity patterns to mitigate the risk of various diseases. Methods Study population and ethics approval The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is a program of studies designed to assess the health and nutritional status of adults and children in the United States 15 . For this research, data were derived from the six continuous NHANES cycles from 2007–2008 to 2017–2018, including a total of 59,842 individuals. Participants with incomplete information on the TyG-index (n = 21,940), physical activity (n = 7382), and other pivotal covariates (n = 14,080) were included in the final analysis. Finally, the data of 16,440 participants were utilized for subsequent analyses. Informed consent was obtained from all participants before the interview and examination, thus additional ethical review board approval was waived to analyze the anonymized NHANES data 16 . The flowchart of participant screening is presented in Fig. 1 . Outcome ascertainment The TyG was calculated with the following formula 17 , in which fasting triglycerides and fasting glucose were expressed in mg/dl: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\text{TyG}} = \ln \frac{fasting\; triglycerides \times fasting\; glucose}{2}$$\end{document} Each eligible participant underwent a telephone health interview to complete a questionnaire and completed a physical examination at a mobile screening center (MEC) 18 . An automated biochemistry analyser was used to determine triglyceride levels and fasting glucose levels enzymatically. The Roche Cobas 6000 Chemistry Analyser and the Roche Modular P are optimized for workloads via a combination of photometric and ion-selective electrode determination (c501 module) and electrochemiluminescence technology for detecting triglyceride concentrations 18 . PA and other covariates PA was evaluated with a questionnaire in which participants were asked about the frequency and duration of vigorous and moderate athletic, fitness, and leisure pursuits which lasted a minimum of 10 uninterrupted minutes during a typical week. PA measurement was computed through the integration of both frequency (expressed as weekly occurrence) and duration (individual duration per episode). The aggregate PA score was determined via formula 2 * vigorous PA + moderate PA. According to the PA guidelines 1 , it is generally accepted for adults that engaging in 2 min of moderate-intensity PA is equivalent to engaging in 1 min of vigorous-intensity PA. Therefore, as previously reported, PA patterns were classified into four categories based on their PA levels 19 – 21 : inactive (devoid of strenuous or moderate PA), insufficiently active (less than 150 min per week of overall PA), weekend warriors (WWs) (at least 150 min per week of overall PA in 1 or 2 sessions), and regularly active (RA) (at least 150 min per week of overall PA in more than two sessions). Previous studies have shown that age, gender, race, education, marital status, poverty income ratio (PIR), body mass index (BMI), smoking status, alcohol use, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and diabetes mellitus have been identified as covariates potentially associated with the TyG index 20 – 22 . On the basis of information provided by NHANES, we categorized races as Mexican American, non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, and Other or Multiracial. Age was categorized as ≤ 45, 45–65, and > 65 years as previously reported 21 . Educational attainment was categorized into five levels: less than 9th grade, 9th-11th grade, high school graduate or equivalent, some college/AA degree, and college graduate or above. Marital status was categorized as married or living with a partner, divorced, separated or widowed, and never married. PIR was categorized into three levels based on previous studies 21 , 23 : < 1.30, 1.30–3.49, and ≥ 3.50. A higher PIR indicates greater family income, whereas a lower PIR signifies increased poverty. Participants were further divided into three groups by BMI based on the criterion from World Health Organization (WHO) 24 , including normal or low body weight (< 25 kg/m 2 ), overweight (25–30 kg/m 2 ), and obese (> 30 kg/m 2 ). Participants can be classified as having diabetes based on the criteria established by the American Diabetes Association (ADA), which includes self-reported diagnoses, the use of insulin or oral hypoglycemic medications, a fasting blood glucose (FBG) level of 126 mg/dL or higher, or an HbA1c level of 6.5% or above, as previously outlined 25 , 26 . Regarding the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease (CVD), participants were asked, "Has a doctor or other health professional ever told you that you have CHF, CHD, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction (MI), or stroke?" Individuals who answered “yes” to any of these questions were categorized as having CVD 25 , 27 . Smoking status was categorized into three groups—never smokers, former smokers, and current smokers—based on information obtained from the self-reported questionnaire, as previously outlined 20 . Individuals who had never smoked 100 cigarettes in their lifetime were classified as never smokers.

Individuals who had never smoked 100 cigarettes in their lifetime were classified as never smokers. Those who had smoked 100 cigarettes at some point but had since quit were identified as former smokers. In contrast, individuals who had smoked 100 cigarettes and continued to smoke were classified as current smokers. Drinking status was similarly categorized into three groups based on the previously described criteria 20 , including never drinkers, former drinkers, and current drinkers. Individuals who had consumed fewer than 12 alcoholic drinks in their lifetime were classified as never drinkers. Those who had consumed 12 or more drinks at some point but had since stopped drinking were identified as former drinkers. Meanwhile, individuals who had consumed 12 or more drinks in their lifetime and had at least one drink in the past 12 months were classified as current drinkers. Statistical analysis Considering the characteristics of complex, multistage sampling design of the NHANES, appropriate sample weights, strata as well as cluster variables were employed. The National Center for Health Statistics recommends that the two-year weight of the MEC be divided by six for statistical purposes, which accounts for the characteristics of data from six successive NHANES cycles and ensures that the data are representative of the general population. All analyses were performed using the statistical software package R ( https://cran.r-project.org/doc/FAQ/R-FAQ.html#Citing-R ). P values less than 0.05 (two-sided) were considered statistically significant. The differences in baseline characteristics among different PA pattern groups were compared by using Rao-Scott chi-squared test or Kruskal–Wallis test. The relationship between PA patterns and the TyG index were analysed through univariate and multivariate linear regression models. Three regression models were established, including model 1 (no covariate was adjusted), model 2 (demographic variables were adjusted, including gender, age, BMI, PIR, race, education, and marital status), and model 3 (additionally adjusted for variables of smoking, drinking, CVD, diabetes and hypertension based on model 2). Moreover, for the identification of potential non-linear relationship between PA and the TyG index, the restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was employed as previously described 28 . Additionally, subgroup analyses and interaction tests were further performed to confirm the correlation between PA and the TyG index based on the stratification of predetermined potential effect modifiers, including age, gender, race, education level, marital status, PIR, BMI, smoking status, alcohol use, CVD, and diabetes.

Results Baseline characteristics of the study population The baseline characteristics of the participants based on PA groups are presented in Table 1 . The study analysed data from 16,440 participants, including 12,909 inactive individuals, 164 insufficiently active individuals, 118 weekend warriors, and 3,249 regularly active individuals. All variables, including gender, age, race, education, marital status, PIR, diabetes status, smoking, alcohol use, BMI, and CVD, were found to be associated with PA patterns. Specifically, adults in the WWs group were more likely to be male, less than 45 years old, non-Hispanic white, have higher education level, be married or living with a partner, have a PIR between 1.3 and 3.5, have lower BMI level, be never smokers, be nonalcoholic, and without history of CVD or diabetes (Table 1 ). Relationship between PA pattern and the TyG index The baseline characteristics of physical activity according to PA patterns was presented in Table 2 . The total MVPA levels for insufficiently active, WWs, and RA adults were 120 min (95% CI 90–140), 290 min (95% CI 180–360), and 540 min (95% CI 360–900), respectively. Figure 2 showed the level of TyG index among different PA pattern groups. Multivariate linear regression models were utilized to explore the association between PA patterns and TyG index, and the results were presented in Table 3 . When the inactive group were defined as reference group, all non-inactive groups reap a significant reduction in TyG index in the non-adjusted model (Model 1), but only the regularly active group remained significant after further adjustment of potential confounding covariates, with the β = −0.05 ( P = 0.3524), − 0.01 ( P = 0.9129), and − 0.11 ( P < 0.0001) for insufficiently active, WWs, and RA, respectively. Conversely, when the regularly active group was defined as the reference group, being WWs was significantly associated with notable TyG index increase in all models (Model 1, β = 0.32, P < 0.0001; Model 2, β = 0.13, P < 0.0001; Model 3, β = 0.11, P < 0.0001). Notably, significant differences in the TyG index were found in non-inactive groups in model 3 regardless of the defining of reference group (all P for trend < 0.0001) (Fig. 3 ). Taken together, the above-mentioned results suggested that only being regularly active, instead of being WWs, was associated significant TyG index reduction.

Stratified analyses according to covariates In order to further verify the robustness and stability of the PA-TyG index association, subgroup analyses based on vital covariates were performed. As presented in Table 4 , the relationships between PA patterns and TyG index remained consistent across different subgroups stratified by the variables of race, age, BMI, PIR, marital status, smoking, drinking, CVD and hypertension. Additionally, interaction tests demonstrated that the associations between PA patterns and TyG index were modified by covariates of diabetes, education and gender (all P interaction < 0.05), and participants being male, with higher education levels, and without diabetes in the regularly active group obtained more pronounced TyG index reduction as opposed to their counterparts. Non-linear relationship between total PA and TyG index RCS analysis were employed to explore the potential non-linear relationship between total PA per week and TyG index in different PA pattern subgroups. The results, as depicted in Fig. 4 , revealed a significant, non-linear, and negative association between total PA per week and TyG index in non-active ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.054) and regularly active ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.118) individuals. The results, as depicted in Fig. 4 , revealed a significant, non-linear, and negative association between total PA per week and TyG index in non-active ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.054) and regularly active ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.118) individuals. Discussion This study aimed to explore the association between different PA patterns and the TyG index. We conducted cross-sectional analyses using nationally representative data, and the results of this study suggest that the majority of U.S. adults reported no participation in PA, with exercise mostly less than 150 min per week. Compared with the inactivity pattern, even the amount of physical activity that did not meet the recommended standard was associated with a lower TyG index. Moreover, the TyG index was significantly lower in both the weekend warrior pattern and regular activity pattern populations than in the inactive population. additionally, our study revealed that being weekend warriors did not reap significant TyG index reduction comparable to being regularly active. Nevertheless, although being non-significant, the weekend warrior pattern indeed bring some benefits in lowering TyG index, which means that the weekend warrior approach can provide a practical alternative for individuals who are unable to engage in regular exercise. To our knowledge, although the pivotal role of PA in alleviating insulin resistance is widely acknowledged, the effect of different PA patterns on IR is scarcely explored. Our study is the first study to analyze and explore the relationship between PA patterns and TyG index. TyG index is not just a reflective marker of insulin resistance 29 , but also serves as biomarker for the onset, progression and prognosis of various disease, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease 30 , sarcopenia 31 , malignancies 32 , etc.. Moreover, existing evidences have indicated that TyG index is superior to HOMA-IR in various aspects, such as predicting metabolic syndrome and hypogonadism 33 , 34 , identifying IR in Chinese type 2 diabetes with a BMI lower than 35 kg/m 2 35 , evaluating the odds of atherosclerosis in coronary/intra- and extracranial arteries 36 . Therefore, exploring the effect of PA patterns and TyG index has broader reference value.

Previous research has shown that maintaining a WWs lifestyle provides comparable health advantages across several domains. These benefits include a decreased likelihood of experiencing cardiovascular events 37 , lower mortality rates related to all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer 38 , a reduced risk of depressive symptoms 39 , 40 , and a decrease in the visceral adiposity index 19 , among others. However, we discovered that only being RA reap significantly TyG index reduction, while being WWs did not obtain comparable TyG index reduction as expected, which is different from previous findings. This discrepancy might be explained by several factors. Given that the health advantages gained from PA largely rely on three key parameters—frequency, duration, and intensity—any variations in TyG index reduction between the RA group and the WWs group can be examined through these three dimensions. First, previous studies have demonstrated that a minimum exercise threshold is crucial for inducing metabolic changes and effectively managing obesity. Specifically, engaging in physical activity that burns approximately 1200 to 1600 kcal per week—equivalent to moderate physical activity (MPA) three to five times a week, or about 7 to 14 miles—can lead to favorable effects on HDL-C metabolism and a reduced risk of coronary heart disease mortality 41 . Consequently, while individuals in the WWs group may reach a total physical activity level of 150 min, this amount may still be insufficient to produce significant changes in lipid metabolism. Additionally, research by Ryuki Hashida et al. found that engaging in exercise for at least 40 to 45 min per session, three times a week over a period of 12 weeks—whether it be aerobic or resistance training—can lead to significant improvements in hepatic steatosis 42 . This indicates that participating in only two exercise sessions, as seen in the WWs group, may not be sufficient to enhance metabolic health.

Moreover, a previous study indicated that the quantity and frequency of physical activity (PA) are more critical for influencing glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes than the mode or intensity of the activity 43 . Patients are encouraged to increase the number of PA sessions per week rather than focusing on extending the duration of each session or raising the intensity to optimize glycemic control. This suggests that the WWs approach may not be ideal for individuals with metabolic disorders. In addition, research conducted by Suk-Yong Jang et al. indicated that individuals classified as WWs (OR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.02–1.65) have a significantly higher likelihood of developing metabolic syndrome compared to those in the RA group 44 . This finding implies that being in the WWs category may contribute to metabolic disorders, potentially counteracting the positive effects of physical activity. Lastly, earlier research has emphasized that sustained and long-term moderate physical activity (MPA) is essential for reducing excess visceral fat in obese women 45 . This underscores the significance of both the frequency and duration of physical activity each week in combating fat accumulation. In summary, our results preliminary revealed that being regularly active, instead of being weekend warriors, lead to sustainable and significant benefits with regard to controlling TyG index. In summary, our results preliminary revealed that being regularly active, instead of being weekend warriors, lead to sustainable and significant benefits with regard to controlling TyG index. Whilst the precise biological mechanisms underlying the correlation between PA and the TyG index remain unclear, potential pivotal pathways may be associated with IR, a condition characterized by decreased sensitivity and responsiveness to insulin action. Previous studies indicated that children who engage in lower amounts of PA or have prolonged sedentary time exhibit higher levels of insulin and HOMA-IR 46 , 47 , while adults who completed higher levels of PA got lower HOMA-IR levels, indicating the potential of PA to improve insulin sensitivity 48 , 49 . Existing evidences have suggested that PA may affect IR in an direct or indirect manner. For example, PA (even in small amount) was reported to directly induce normalization of glycogen synthesis and IR, reducing hepatic lipid content and de novo lipogenesis 50 . Such effects relied on the complex interactions among different organs, including liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. Besides, PA may also affect IR via various indirect mechanisms, including increasing energy expenditure and improving body composition, reducing adipose tissue inflammation and liver ectopic lipid deposition, enhancing skeletal muscle metabolic capacity, etc. 51 , 52 . Overall, these insights highlight the critical role of physical activity in modulating insulin resistance and underscore the importance of promoting regular physical activity for better metabolic health.

Overall, these insights highlight the critical role of physical activity in modulating insulin resistance and underscore the importance of promoting regular physical activity for better metabolic health. This study has several advantages. Firstly, we used a large dataset including 20,923 participants, which ensured representativeness. Secondly, the study specifically focused on the relationship between different PA patterns and the TyG index, thereby examining the association between insulin resistance and different PA patterns. Finally, the statistical methods of restricted cubic splines analyses, subgroup analyses and interaction tests were utilized to confirm the robustness and stability of the association between PA and TyG index across diverse subgroups. However, some limitations still exist in this study. First, the present study was based on a cross-sectional survey, which did not allow for the determination of a causal relationship between activity patterns and the TyG index. Second, many factors are associated with the TyG index and the variables considered in this study are limited. Third, the self-reported PA data may introduce recall or reporting bias, which could affect the accuracy of the PA classifications and their association with the TyG index. Fourth, this study did not account for dietary habits and calorie intake, potential confounding variables that may affect the TyG index. Future research should address these factors. In conclusion, our findings emphasize the critical role of PA in enhancing insulin sensitivity and managing the TyG index. Engaging in regular physical activity throughout the week, rather than solely being WWs, was linked to sustained and significant decreases in the TyG index. Importantly, while WWs did not lead to lasting and significant reductions in the TyG index after controlling for established confounding factors, they still provided some degree of improvement for individuals who participated in them. Therefore, for those with limited time for regular exercise, incorporating WWs can still offer benefits for improving and maintaining metabolic health.
